    T000002Countably compact ⇒ Weakly countably compactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Countably compact
    Then
    Weakly countably compact

    Let A⊂XA \subset X be countably infinite. If A⊂XA \subset X has no limit point then it must be closed. Moreover, for every a∈Aa \in A there is some open Ua⊂XU_a \subset X such that Ua∩A={a}U_a \cap A = \{a\}. Then the set of all UaU_a together with X∖AX \setminus A forms a countable cover of XX and must have some finite subcover. Thus AA may be covered by finitely many UaU_a, contradicting the fact that AA is infinite. Thus AA must have a limit point.

    Asserted on page 21 of Counterexamples in Topology.

    Sources cited by Pi-Base

    • Counterexamples in Topology

    Original Pi-Base record and proof · Pinned source · Permalink

    T000003Sequentially compact ⇒ Countably compactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Sequentially compact
    Then
    Countably compact

    If XX is not countably compact then there is some countable open cover {Un}n∈ω\{U_n\}_{n \in \omega} of XX with no finite subcover. Let xn∈X∖∪i<nUi≠∅x_n \in X \setminus \cup_{i < n} U_i \neq \emptyset for all n∈ωn \in \omega. Then for any p∈Xp \in X, p∈Unp \in U_n for some least nn and so no infinite subsequence of {xn}\{x_n\} converges to pp.

    Asserted on page 21 of Counterexamples in Topology.

    Sources cited by Pi-Base

    • Counterexamples in Topology

    Original Pi-Base record and proof · Pinned source · Permalink

    T000004Countably compact ⇒ PseudocompactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Countably compact
    Then
    Pseudocompact

    If XX is countably compact and f:X→ℝf:X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, the collection of all sets f−1((−n,n))f^{-1}((-n,n)) for n∈ωn \in \omega forms a countable cover of XX and so has a finite subcover. Thus there is some maximal r∈ωr \in \omega so that X⊂f−1((−r,r))X \subset f^{-1}((-r,r)) and so ff is bounded.

    Asserted on page 21 of Counterexamples in Topology.

    Sources cited by Pi-Base

    T000027(Weakly locally compact ∧ R1R_1) ⇒ Completely regularFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    T000028(T2T_2 ∧ Countably compact ∧ First countable) ⇒ T3T_3Formula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    ($T_2$ ∧ Countably compact ∧ First countable)
    Then
    $T_3$

    Suppose we have a closed set AA and a point x∉Ax\notin A. Let (Un)n∈ℕ(U_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}} be a countable neighbourhood basis for xx. Since XX is T2T_2, the (countably many) open sets X∖Un‾X\setminus\overline{U_n} cover AA. Since AA is closed in XX, it is also Countably compact; consequently A⊆⋃n∈I(X∖Un‾)A\subseteq\bigcup_{n\in I}(X\setminus\overline{U_n}) for some finite I⊆ℕI\subseteq\mathbb N. Taking complements, one sees that ⋂n∈IUn‾\bigcap_{n\in I}\overline{U_n}, which is a closed neighborhood of xx, is disjoint from AA.

    Original Pi-Base record and proof · Pinned source · Permalink

Since each member of $ \mathcal{V}$ meets some NxnN_{x_n}, 𝒱\mathcal{V} is necessarily countable.)

    T000107(Countably compact ∧ Meta-Lindelöf) ⇒ CompactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Countably compact ∧ Meta-Lindelöf)
    Then
    Compact

    Theorem 1 and the following Remark of A note on compactness and metacompactness (Boyte) show that in any topological space admitting a point-countable open cover without a countable subcover, one can construct a sequence without an accumulation point; and thus such a space cannot be Countably compact.

    Now let 𝒰\mathcal U be an open cover of XX. If XX is Meta-Lindelöf, 𝒰\mathcal U has a point-countable open refinement 𝒱\mathcal V. If XX is also Countably compact, 𝒱\mathcal V has a countable subcover by the previous paragraph; and by Countably compact again, 𝒱\mathcal V has a finite subcover, which is a finite open refinement of 𝒰\mathcal U. This proves XX is Compact.

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    $\sigma$-compact
    Then
    Markov Menger

    See the proof of Theorem 2.2 in The combinatorics of open covers II, which we summarize here.

    An ω\omega-cover of a compact space admits a finite subcover that covers all kk-sized subsets for any positive integer kk. Write the space XX as an ascending union of {Kn:n∈ω}\{K_n:n\in\omega\} where each KnK_n is compact. Given an ω\omega-cover 𝒰n\mathscr U_n of XX, let 𝒱n\mathscr V_n be a finite subset of 𝒰n\mathscr U_n that covers all nn-sized subsets of KnK_n. Note that this is a winning Markov strategy in the ω\omega-Menger game (equivalent to Markov Menger).

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    Given a cozero set UU in XX, the open set X∖U‾X\setminus\overline U contains a maximal collection 𝒱\mathscr V of pairwise disjoint nonempty cozero sets of XX. By Countable chain condition 𝒱\mathscr V is countable, hence V=⋃𝒱V=\bigcup\mathscr V is a cozero set. And since XX is Completely regular, the maximality of 𝒱\mathscr V implies that VV is dense in X∖U‾X\setminus\overline U. So VV is a cozero complement of UU.

    T000155Regular ⇒ SemiregularFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    Regular

    Let (X,τ)(X,\tau) be a regular topological space. Let also x∈Xx \in X and V∈τV \in \tau be arbitrary. To show that (X,τ)(X,\tau) has a base of regular open sets, we show there is UU satisfying x∈U⊂Vx \in U \subset V and int⁡(cl⁡(U))=U\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (U)) = U.

    Since x∉Vcx \notin V^c, it follows from regularity that xx and VcV^c can be separated by open sets. Let U0U_0 be the open set containing xx in this separation. Define UU to be int⁡(cl⁡(U0))\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (U_0)).

    Since U0U_0 is open, we know U0⊂UU_0 \subset U, and so x∈Ux \in U.

    Since U0U_0 is a separation of xx from VcV^c, we know cl⁡(U0)⊂V\operatorname{cl}(U_0) \subset V, and so U⊂VU \subset V.

    Finally, int⁡(cl⁡(U))=int⁡(cl⁡(int⁡(cl⁡(U0))))=int⁡(cl⁡(U0))=U\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (U)) = \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (U_0)))) = \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl} (U_0)) = U.

    Asserted in 14E of General Topology (Willard).

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    Given a Locally connected GO-space XX, there is a base for the topology consisting of Connected open sets. Each of these open sets UU is itself a GO-space (as a subspace of a GO-space), hence is a LOTS by (GO-space ∧ Connected) ⇒ LOTS.     T000216GO-space ⇒ RadialFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    GO-space
    Then
    Radial

    The result for LOTS is stated as evident in the first sentence of the proof of Satz 1 in Quotienten geordneter Räume und Folgenkonvergenz (H. Herrlich).

    Given a subset AA of a LOTS space XX, a point p∈A‾∖Ap\in\overline A\setminus A is in the closure of the part of AA to one side of pp, say the left side. So the set B={a∈A:a<p}B=\{a\in A:a<p\} has no maximum point and is cofinal in the set of points of XX to the left of pp. As BB is totally ordered, it admits a well-ordered cofinal subset and that set corresponds to a transfinite sequence of points of AA converging to pp.

    And since Radial is a hereditary property, the result also holds for GO-space.

    T000236(GO-space ∧ Countably tight) ⇒ First countableFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (GO-space ∧ Countably tight)
    Then
    First countable

    Shown by KP Hart at Is there a generalized order space $X$ with countable tightness which is not first countable?. To see this, suppose XX is a GO-space for some linear order << and let a∈Xa\in X.

    If aa is not isolated to the left (that is, in (←,a](\leftarrow,a]), it is in the closure of (←,a)(\leftarrow,a) and by Countably tight there is a countably infinite set C⊆(←,a)C\subseteq(\leftarrow,a) with a=sup⁡Ca=\sup C. We can then extract a strictly increasing sequence (xn)(x_n) in CC with a=sup⁡xna=\sup x_n. Similarly, if aa is not isolated to the right, there is a strictly decreasing sequence (yn)(y_n) with a=inf⁡yna=\inf y_n.

    So, if aa is not isolated on either side, any neighborhood of aa contains an order-convex neighborhood, which necessarily contains points on either side of aa, and hence contains an interval (xn,yn)(x_n,y_n). Thus the collection of intervals (xn,yn)(x_n,y_n) forms a countable local base at aa. And if aa is isolated on one side or both, one can take the collection of intervals (xn,a](x_n,a] or [a,yn)[a,y_n) or the singleton {a}\{a\}.

    Sources cited by Pi-Base

    T000274Discrete ⇒ LOTSFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Discrete
    Then
    LOTS

    Since discrete spaces are homeomorphic precisely when they have the same cardinality, it suffices to show that for every cardinality kk there is a set of cardinality kk with a total order that induces the discrete topology.

    Let κ\kappa be a cardinal number. If κ\kappa is finite, then any total order on kk induces the discrete topology. If κ\kappa is infinite, let X=α×ℤX=\alpha \times \mathbb{Z} where α\alpha is an ordinal of cardinality κ\kappa, together with the lexicographical ordering. Then we see that XX with the order topology is discrete.

    See also Verification of basic properties of order topology.

Then the collection of all open intervals and rays of the form (p,q)(p, q) with p,q∈Q∪{−∞,∞}p,q\in Q\cup \{-\infty, \infty\} forms a countable base for XX. To see this, let x∈(a,b)x\in(a,b) - as XX is connected if either of (a,x)(a,x) or (x,b)(x,b) is empty then xx is the minimum (resp maximum) value of XX, so choose p∈(a,x)∩Qp\in(a,x)\cap Q and q∈(x,b)∩Qq\in(x,b)\cap Q if they are nonempty, otherwise choose p=−∞p=-\infty or q=∞q=\infty as necessary.

    T000277(GO-space ∧ Countable chain condition) ⇒ Hereditarily LindelöfFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (GO-space ∧ Countable chain condition)
    Then
    Hereditarily Lindelöf

    For the result with the stronger hypothesis of LOTS in place of GO-space, see Theorem 2.2 in Separability, the countable chain condition and the Lindelöf property in linearly orderable spaces (Lutzer & Bennet).

    The general result with GO-space is Proposition 2.10(b) in On generalized ordered spaces (D. Lutzer) (https://eudml.org/doc/268514) and is proved as follows. Suppose XX is a GO-space satisfying the CCC condition. It can be topologically embedded as a dense subspace of a LOTS YY (see for example Equivalent definitions for GO-spaces (generalized ordered spaces)). Since XX is dense in YY, the space YY also satisfies CCC, hence is Hereditarily Lindelöf by the first result. The conclusion then follows since Hereditarily Lindelöf is a hereditary property.

    For the general result with GO-space, suppose XX is a GO-space satisfying the CCC condition. It can be topologically embedded as a dense subspace of a LOTS YY (see for example Equivalent definitions for GO-spaces (generalized ordered spaces)). Since XX is dense in YY, the space YY also satisfies CCC, hence is First countable by the first result. The conclusion then follows since First countable is a hereditary property.

    T000280(Locally countable ∧ T1T_1) ⇒ Totally path disconnectedFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally countable ∧ $T_1$)
    Then
    Totally path disconnected

    Let II be the interval [0,1][0,1] and consider a path f:I→Xf:I\to X. Suppose first that XX is Countable and T1T_1. Each f−1(x)f^{-1}(x) for x∈Xx\in X is a (possibly empty) closed subset of II. The nonempty f−1(x)f^{-1}(x) partition II into countably many closed sets. The number of these nonempty closed sets cannot be finite >1>1, since II is connected. And as shown in Why are the integers with the cofinite topology not path-connected?, it cannot be countably infinite either (theorem of Sierpiński (1918)). So there is only one such closed set and ff is constant.

    Suppose now that XX is Locally countable and T1T_1. For each t∈It\in I the function ff maps some closed interval around tt to some countable subspace of XX. By the countable case above, ff is constant on that interval; so ff is locally constant. A standard argument using the connectedness of II then implies that ff is constant.

    Sources cited by Pi-Base

    • Why are the integers with the cofinite topology not path-connected?

    If Z1,Z2Z_1, Z_2 are disjoint zero-sets, there exists a continuous f:X→[0,1]f:X\to [0, 1] such that f−1(0)=Z1f^{-1}(0) = Z_1 and f−1(1)=Z2f^{-1}(1) = Z_2 (see theorem 1.5.14 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)). Since ∣X∣<𝔠|X| < \mathfrak{c} there exists r∈(0,1)r\in (0, 1) such that f−1(r)=∅f^{-1}(r) = \emptyset. Then V=f−1([0,r))=f−1([0,r])V = f^{-1}([0, r)) = f^{-1}([0, r]) is a clopen set such that Z1⊆VZ_1\subseteq V and Z2∩V=∅Z_2\cap V = \emptyset, so XX is Strongly zero-dimensional.

    T000307(Locally finite ∧ T0T_0) ⇒ ScatteredFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally finite ∧ $T_0$)
    Then
    Scattered

    First assume XX is nonempty and show it has an isolated point. Take a nonempty finite open set U⊆XU\subseteq X that is minimal under inclusion. It cannot contain more than one point, otherwise intersecting with another open set that contains one point and not another in UU would give a strictly smaller open set, which is not possible. So UU consists of one isolated point.

    Now given any nonempty subspace A⊆XA\subseteq X, it is itself locally finite and T0T_0 and hence contains a point isolated in AA. This shows that XX is scattered.

    T000348(Has a group topology ∧ First countable) ⇒ PseudometrizableFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If

    Then

    This is essentially the Birkhoff-Kakutani theorem (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2011/05/17/the-birkhoff-kakutani-theorem/), which says that a topological group is metrizable if and only if it is Hausdorff and first countable. The current version without Hausdorff is obtained by passing to the Kolmogorov quotient.

    One way to prove it is to show that a uniformity on a set is induced by a pseudometric if it has a countable base. And if a topological group is first countable, the usual left (or right) uniformity on the group has a countable base.

    See Theorem 38.3 and Problem 38C(1) in General Topology (Willard), or Theorem 8.1.21 and Exercise 8.1.G in General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

    T000375kk-Menger ⇒ ω\omega-MengerFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    $k$-Menger
    Then
    $\omega$-Menger

    Theorem 6 of Applications of k-covers states that a space XX is kk-Menger if and only if XmX^m is kk-Menger for every positive integer mm. To see that a kk-Menger space is Menger in each of its finite powers, it suffices to see that a space being kk-Menger is Menger. Indeed, given any sequence ⟨𝒰n:n∈ω⟩\langle \mathscr U_n : n \in \omega \rangle of open covers of a kk-Menger space XX, we can form 𝒱n\mathscr V_n to be the finite unions of elements of 𝒰n\mathscr U_n. Then 𝒱n\mathscr V_n is a kk-cover of XX. We can apply the kk-Menger selection principle to produce a kk-cover of XX and note that such a selection corresponds to finite selections from each 𝒰n\mathscr U_n which result in a cover of XX.

    T000388GδG_\delta space ⇒ Countably metacompactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    $G_\delta$ space
    Then
    Countably metacompact

    We will use Ishikawa's characterization of Countably metacompact.

    Suppose XX is GδG_\delta space. Let F0⊇F1⊇⋯F_0 \supseteq F_1 \supseteq \cdots be a nested sequence of closed sets with empty intersection. Since each FnF_n is a GδG_\delta set, Fn=⋂m∈ωUn,mF_n = \bigcap_{m \in \omega} U_{n, m} for some open sets Un,mU_{n, m}.

    Define Uk:=⋂n≤k,m≤kUn,mU_k := \bigcap_{n \leq k, m \leq k} U_{n, m}. Clearly each UkU_k is an open set and Fk=⋂n≤kFn=⋂n≤k,m∈ωUn,m⊆UkF_k = \bigcap_{n \leq k} F_n = \bigcap_{n \leq k, m \in \omega} U_{n, m} \subseteq U_k. Finally, ⋂k∈ωUk=⋂n∈ω,m∈ωUn,m=⋂n∈ωFn=∅\bigcap_{k \in \omega} U_k = \bigcap_{n \in \omega, m \in \omega} U_{n, m} = \bigcap_{n \in \omega} F_n = \varnothing.

    Therefore, XX is Countably metacompact.

    T000445(Compact ∧ Connected ∧ LOTS ∧ ¬ Empty) ⇒ Fixed point propertyFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Compact ∧ Connected ∧ LOTS ∧ ¬Empty)
    Then
    Fixed point property

    Let f ⁣:X→Xf\colon X\to X be continuous. For x0∈Xx_0\in X, if f(x0)>x0f(x_0)>x_0, then let U,VU,V be disjoint open neighborhoods with x0∈Ux_0\in U, f(x0)∈Vf(x_0)\in V, and u<vu<v for each u∈Uu\in U, v∈Vv\in V. Then for x∈f−1(V)∩Ux\in f^{-1}(V)\cap U, f(x)>xf(x)>x, so A:={x∈X∣f(x)>x}A:=\{x\in X\mid f(x)>x\} is open, as is B:={x∈X∣f(x)<x}B:=\{x\in X\mid f(x)<x\}.

    If ff has no fixed point, then X=A∪BX=A\cup B, and since XX is Connected, AA or BB must be empty. But if X=AX=A, then XX has no maximum element, and likewise if X=BX=B, it has no minimum element.

    This contradicts that if XX is LOTS and Compact and not Empty, then it has a maximum and minimum element, by the remark in Answer to "Use compactness to prove that a closed bounded set of real numbers has a maximum".

    For the general result, suppose XX is a GO-space that is Second countable.     T000470(Partition topology ∧ Homogeneous ∧ ¬ Empty) ⇒ Has a group topologyFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Partition topology ∧ Homogeneous ∧ ¬Empty)
    Then
    Has a group topology

    The partition elements of a Homogeneous Partition topology space must all have the same cardinality, so the space is a product of a Discrete space and an Indiscrete space. Given any nonzero cardinal, there is a group with that cardinality (for example, a cyclic group in the finite case and ⊕k∈κℤ\oplus_{k\in\kappa}\mathbb{Z} for infinite cardinal κ\kappa). When the group is given either the discrete or indiscrete topology, the group operations are continuous. Thus, the topological product of them admits a compatible group structure from the product group of the two.

    T000536(Locally Euclidean ∧ Connected) ⇒ Locally nn-EuclideanFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally Euclidean ∧ Connected)
    Then
    Locally $n$-Euclidean

    If a point xx has at the same time an open neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝn\mathbb R^n and an open neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝm\mathbb R^m with n≠mn\ne m, their intersection would be homeomorphic to an open set in ℝn\mathbb R^n and to an open set in ℝm\mathbb R^m. But this is not possible by invariance of domain (Invariance of domain on Wikipedia). So the dimension nn at the point xx is completely determined by the point, and by definition of Locally Euclidean the set of points of a given dimension nn is open in XX. Since XX is Connected, the dimension must be the same at every point.

    T000542Shrinking ⇒ NormalFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Shrinking
    Then
    Normal

    The argument in Generalized paracompactness (Y. Yasui) for this result goes as follows. Suppose EE and FF are disjoint closed subsets of a shrinking space XX. Then {X∖E,X∖F}\{ X \setminus E , X \setminus F\} is an open cover of XX, so there exists an open cover {U,V}\{U, V\} of XX such that U‾⊆X∖E\overline{U} \subseteq X \setminus E and V‾⊆X∖F\overline{V} \subseteq X \setminus F. Note then that E⊆X∖U‾E \subseteq X \setminus \overline{U}, F⊆X∖V‾F \subseteq X \setminus \overline{V}, and (X∖U‾)∩(X∖V‾)=X∖(U‾∪V‾)=∅\left( X \setminus \overline{U} \right) \cap \left( X \setminus \overline{V} \right) = X \setminus \left( \overline{U} \cup \overline{V} \right) = \emptyset.

    See also Dan Ma's Topology Blog post on Spaces with shrinking properties.

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    Then

    Suppose by contradiction that XX is not Totally path disconnected, that is, there is a non-constant path f:[0,1]→Xf:[0,1]\to X. Its range f([0,1])f([0,1]) is Path connected and Weak Hausdorff, hence Arc connected (Explore). So there is a homeomorphic embedding g:[0,1]→Xg:[0,1]\to X. Since gg is a continuous map from a compact Hausdorff space to a Weak Hausdorff space, its image g([0,1])g([0,1]) is closed in XX, hence Rothberger.

    This implies that Unit interval [0,1][0,1] is Rothberger. But this is not the case, by a simple measure argument as used for example in How to show that $\mathbb R$ is not Rothberger, and that it is Menger.

Otherwise, if p∉Ap \notin A, then F−1(A)=A×{0}F^{-1}(A) = A \times \{0\}. Since F−1(A)F^{-1}(A) is closed in both cases, it follows that FF is continuous.

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    (Ultraconnected ∧ Shrinking ∧ ¬Empty)
    Then
    Has a point with a unique neighborhood

    Assume to the contrary that XX is not Has a point with a unique neighborhood. The intersection of {x}‾\overline{\{x\}} for all x∈Xx \in X coincides with the intersection of all nonempty closed sets, so it is the set of all focal points of XX, whence empty by assumption. Thus, {{x}‾c:x∈X}\{\overline{\{x\}}^c: x \in X\} is an open cover of XX. As XX is Shrinking, there is an open cover {Vx}x∈X\{V_x\}_{x \in X} of XX s.t. Vx‾⊆{x}‾c\overline{V_x} \subseteq \overline{\{x\}}^c for all xx. Now, fix x0∈Xx_0 \in X. There exists x∈Xx \in X s.t. x0∈Vx⊆Vx‾⊆{x}‾cx_0 \in V_x \subseteq \overline{V_x} \subseteq \overline{\{x\}}^c. Then Vx‾\overline{V_x} and {x}‾\overline{\{x\}} are nonempty disjoint closed sets, which contradicts XX being Ultraconnected.

    T000641(Locally relatively compact ∧ T0T_0 ∧ ¬ Empty) ⇒ Has a closed pointFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally relatively compact ∧ $T_0$ ∧ ¬Empty)
    Then
    Has a closed point

    Since the space XX is nonempty and Locally relatively compact, it has a nonempty closed Compact subset YY. Now, as YY is compact, any chain of nonempty closed subsets of YY has nonempty intersection. Thus, by Zorn's lemma, there is a minimal nonempty closed subset AA of YY. Since YY is closed in XX, so is AA, and thus AA is a minimal nonempty closed subset of XX. As XX is T0T_0, it is easy to see that AA must be a singleton.

    T000669Metrizable ⇒ Monotonically normalFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Metrizable
    Then
    Monotonically normal

    Let (X,d)(X,d) be a metric space. Write B(x,ϵ)B(x,\epsilon) for the open ball centered at xx with radius ϵ\epsilon.

    The space is T1T_1.

    For x∈Ux\in U with UU open in XX, define μ(x,U)\mu(x,U) to be some open ball B(x,ϵ)B(x,\epsilon), ϵ>0\epsilon>0, such that B(x,2ϵ)⊆UB(x,2\epsilon)\subseteq U. If B(x,ϵ1)∩B(y,ϵ2)≠∅B(x,\epsilon_1)\cap B(y,\epsilon_2)\ne\emptyset with ϵ2≤ϵ1\epsilon_2\le\epsilon_1, necessarily y∈B(x,2ϵ1)y\in B(x,2\epsilon_1) by the triangle inequality. So μ(x,U)\mu(x,U) satisfies Definition (2) of Monotonically normal.

    T000670(Countably paracompact ∧ Hyperconnected) ⇒ Countably compactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Countably paracompact ∧ Hyperconnected)
    Then
    Countably compact

    Let 𝒰\mathscr U be a countable open cover of XX. Let 𝒱\mathscr V be a locally finite open refinement of 𝒰\mathscr U covering XX. Given a point x∈Xx\in X, there is an open neighborhood WW of xx that intersects only finitely many members of 𝒱\mathscr V. But since XX is Hyperconnected, WW intersects all (nonempty) members of 𝒱\mathscr V; hence 𝒱\mathscr V is finite. That is sufficient to conclude that 𝒰\mathscr U has a finite subcover.

    T000685(Topological nn-manifold ∧ Compact ∧ Has multiple points) ⇒ ¬ ContractibleFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Topological $n$-manifold ∧ Compact ∧ Has multiple points)
    Then
    ¬Contractible

    Let MM be a Compact Contractible nn-manifold. Since Contractible spaces are Connected (Explore), MM is a connected closed nn-manifold (where "closed manifold" here means a "compact manifold without boundary"; see wikipedia Closed_manifold). It follows from the remark after Theorem 3.26 in the Poincaré duality section of Algebraic Topology (Hatcher) that Hn(M;ℤ2)=ℤ2H_n(M; \mathbb Z_2) = \mathbb Z_2.

    But since MM is Contractible, we have Hn(M;ℤ2)=0H_n(M; \mathbb Z_2) = 0 for all n≥1n \geq 1. This forces n=0n = 0 and therefore MM is The Singleton.

    See also Is there a compact contractible manifold?.

    T000686(Metacompact ∧ Collectionwise normal ∧ Regular) ⇒ ParacompactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Metacompact ∧ Collectionwise normal ∧ Regular)
    Then
    Paracompact

    This is the Michael-Nagami theorem.

    According to Theorem 5.3.3 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989) (which assumes T2T_2 for all notions in that chapter), spaces that are Metacompact, Collectionwise normal and T2T_2 are Paracompact. By passing to the Kolmogorov quotient, one obtains that Metacompact Collectionwise normal R1R_1 spaces are Paracompact.

    Now Collectionwise normal implies Normal. And for Normal spaces, the properties R0R_0, R1R_1 and Regular are equivalent (Explore). So one can equivalently formulate the theorem with the Regular property.

    OPEN QUESTION: Is the Regular hypothesis needed?

    • a particular point topology (like Particular point topology on a countably infinite set), which is hyperconnected;
    • a free ultrafilter topology (like Free ultrafilter topology on ω\omega), which is hyperconnected.

    Then

    T000748First countable ⇒ α1\alpha_1Formula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    First countable
    Then
    $\alpha_1$

    Stated on p. 94 of Subsets of ${}^\omega\omega$ and the Fréchet-Urysohn and $\alpha_i$-properties (P. Nyikos).

    Let x∈Xx\in X and let S1,S2,⋯⊆XS_1, S_2, \dots\subseteq X be countably infinite sets, each converging to xx. Since XX is First countable, the point xx has a countable local base of neighborhoods V1⊇V2⊇…V_1\supseteq V_2\supseteq\dots. As SnS_n converges to xx, the set Tn=Sn∩VnT_n=S_n\cap V_n is cofinite in SnS_n and also converges to xx.

    Claim: The set S=⋃n=1∞TnS=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty T_n is as required in the definition of α1\alpha_1:

    • (1) S∩Sn⊇TnS\cap S_n\supseteq T_n is cofinite in SnS_n for each nn.
    • (2) To show that SS converges to xx, consider a basic neighborhood VmV_m of xx for some fixed mm. If n≥mn\ge m, we have Tn⊆Vn⊆VmT_n\subseteq V_n\subseteq V_m. And for the finitely many n<mn<m, VmV_m contains all but finitely many elements of TnT_n since TnT_n converges to xx. Therefore, VmV_m contains all but finitely many elements of SS. This shows that SS converges to xx.

If x∈Cx\in C, then r:=d(x,A)=d(x,B)>0r := d(x, A) = d(x, B) > 0 so that d(x,y)<rd(x, y) < r implies d(y,A)=d(x,A)=d(x,B)=d(y,B)d(y, A) = d(x, A) = d(x, B) = d(y, B), and therefore B(x,r)⊆CB(x, r)\subseteq C.     T000798Has a cofinite topology ⇒ W-spaceFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Has a cofinite topology
    Then
    W-space

    Player 1 can play the W-game at a point x∈Xx\in X by choosing U0=XU_0=X. And at round nn, if Player 2 chose xi∈Uix_i\in U_i at round ii for i=0,...,n−1i=0,...,n-1, Player 1 can choose Un=(X∖{x0,…,xn−1})∪{x}U_n=(X\setminus\{x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}\})\cup\{x\}, which is an open neighborhood of xx.

    Each element y≠xy\ne x can appear at most once in the sequence (xn)n(x_n)_n. From this, it follows that xn→xx_n\to x and Player 1 wins.

    T000799(Has a cofinite topology ∧ Subparacompact) ⇒ CountableFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Has a cofinite topology ∧ Subparacompact)
    Then
    Countable

    Let 𝒱\mathscr V be a locally finite collection of subsets of XX. Then 𝒱\mathscr V must be finite. Indeed, there is an open cofinite set UU meeting only finitely many elements of 𝒱\mathscr V; and any other element of 𝒱\mathscr V is contained in the (finite) complement of UU, and so there are only finitely many of them. And consequently, any σ\sigma-locally finite collection of subsets of XX must be countable.

    Now let 𝒰\mathscr U be a σ\sigma-locally finite closed refinement of the open cover {X∖{p}∣p∈X}\left\{ X \setminus \{p\} \mid p \in X \right\}. Every element of 𝒰\mathscr U is a closed proper subset of XX, hence finite. And 𝒰\mathscr U is countable. Therefore, X=⋃𝒰X=\bigcup\mathscr U is countable.

    Original Pi-Base record and proof · Pinned source · Permalink

    By taking the Kolmogorov quotient we might assume that XX is locally compact Hausdorff. The general case follows from t(X)≤t(αX)≤s(αX)=s(X)t(X) \leq t(\alpha X) \leq s(\alpha X) = s(X) where αX\alpha X is the one-point compactification of XX.

    T000813(Sequentially discrete ∧ Scattered ∧ k1k_1-Hausdorff) ⇒ AnticompactFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Sequentially discrete ∧ Scattered ∧ $k_1$-Hausdorff)
    Then
    Anticompact

    Let KK be a Compact subset of XX. Then KK is T2T_2 (since XX is k1k_1-Hausdorff), and KK is also Sequentially discrete and Scattered. To show that KK is finite, without loss of generality we can assume that XX itself is Compact, T2T_2, Sequentially discrete and Scattered and show that XX is finite.

    If every point of XX is isolated, XX is finite by compactness. Otherwise, because XX is Scattered, choose x∈Xx \in X with Cantor–Bendixson rank 11 (that is, x∈X′∖X′′x\in X'\setminus X''). So xx is not isolated in XX and there is a neighbourhood LL of xx such that all points in L∖{x}L\setminus\{x\} are isolated in XX. Since XX is Regular, we can assume LL is closed in XX. The neighbourhood LL must be infinite, because otherwise xx would be isolated.

    Take a countably infinite set M⊆LM\subseteq L containing xx. Since LL is Almost discrete, MM is closed in LL, hence closed in XX and compact. And since MM is Sequentially discrete and Compact, it is not Countably infinite (Explore), which is a contradiction.

    Original Pi-Base record and proof · Pinned source · Permalink

    T000842(Locally a Euclidean half-space ∧ Connected) ⇒ Locally an nn-Euclidean half-spaceFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally a Euclidean half-space ∧ Connected)
    Then
    Locally an $n$-Euclidean half-space

    Suppose a point xx has at the same time an open neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+, and an open neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of ℝ+m\mathbb R^m_+ with n≠mn\ne m. Their intersection UU is a nonempty open set in XX which is homeomorphic to an open set in ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ and to an open set in ℝ+m\mathbb R^m_+.

    Every nonempty open set in ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ contains a nonempty open set homeomorphic to an open set in ℝn\mathbb R^n. So there is a nonempty open set V⊆UV\subseteq U homeomorphic to an open set in ℝn\mathbb R^n. Since VV is also homeomorphic to an open set in ℝ+m\mathbb R^m_+, there is a nonempty open set W⊆VW\subseteq V homeomorphic to an open set in ℝm\mathbb R^m (and also to an open set in ℝn\mathbb R^n). But this is not possible by invariance of domain (Invariance of domain on Wikipedia).

    It follows that the dimension nn at the point xx is completely determined by the point, and by definition of Locally a Euclidean half-space the set of points of a given dimension nn is open in XX. Since XX is Connected, the dimension must be the same at every point.

    T000846(Locally orderable ∧ Locally path connected ∧ ¬ Has an isolated point) ⇒ Locally a Euclidean half-lineFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    (Locally orderable ∧ Locally path connected ∧ ¬Has an isolated point)
    Then
    Locally a Euclidean half-line

    The empty space is vacuously Locally a Euclidean half-line. Now assume X≠∅X\ne\emptyset and let x∈Xx\in X. There is an open neighborhood UU of xx that is orderable (LOTS), and a Path connected open neighborhood VV of xx with V⊆UV\subseteq U. Since a connected set in a LOTS is order-convex, VV is also a LOTS with the order ≤\le induced from UU.

    Take a neighborhood of xx in (V,≤)(V,\le) of the form [p,q][p,q] for some p≤x≤qp\le x\le q; necessarily p<qp<q because xx is not isolated in VV. The interval [p,q]⊆V[p,q]\subseteq V is homeomorphic to the interval [0,1]⊆ℝ[0,1]\subseteq\mathbb R (see Answer to "Are path-connected LOTS also locally path-connected?"). From this, it is easy to obtain a neighborhood of xx homeomorphic to Interval [0,1)[0,1). That is, XX is Locally a Euclidean half-line.

    Suppose XX is Path connected and a LOTS with the linear order ≤\le. Let f:S1→Xf:S^1\to X be a continuous map.     T000909(Well-based ∧ Has countable π\pi-character ∧ R0R_0) ⇒ First countableFormula

WLOG assume xx is not isolated (otherwise {{x}}\{\{x\}\} is a countable local base for xx). Therefore, for any A∈𝒜A \in \mathcal{A}, there is some a∈A∖{x}a \in A \setminus \{x\}. By T1T_1 we can choose some UA∈𝒰U_A\in\mathscr U that avoids the point aa; hence A⊈UAA\not\subseteq U_A.

    Clearly, {UA:A∈𝒜}\{U_A: A \in \mathcal{A}\} is a countable family of neighbourhoods of xx; we show that it is cofinal in 𝒰\mathcal{U} with respect to reverse inclusion, hence a local base for xx. If U∈𝒰U \in \mathcal{U}, there is A∈𝒜A \in \mathcal{A} with A⊆UA \subseteq U, but since A⊈UAA \not \subseteq U_A, we cannot have U⊆UAU \subseteq U_A. By the hypothesis that 𝒰\mathcal{U} is linearly ordered by inclusion, we must have UA⊂UU_A \subset U instead. This concludes the proof for the T1T_1 case.

    Sober Alexandrov Noetherian spaces are Finite (Explore). Therefore, the desired result follows by passing to the Kolmogorov quotient.

    T000937Basically disconnected ⇒ FF-spaceFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    Basically disconnected
    Then
    $F$-space

    If U,V⊆XU, V\subseteq X are disjoint cozero sets, then U‾\overline{U} is a clopen set that separates them. Since clopen sets are zero sets, it follows that U,VU, V are contained in disjoint zero sets.

    T000938(F′F'-space ∧ Cozero complemented) ⇒ Basically disconnectedFormula

    Domain: topological spaces. Read as a universal implication in the Pi-Base theory.

    If
    ($F'$-space ∧ Cozero complemented)
    Then
    Basically disconnected

    If U⊆XU\subseteq X is a cozero set, find a cozero set V⊆XV\subseteq X such that U∪VU\cup V is dense in XX. Then U‾,V‾\overline{U}, \overline{V} are disjoint closed sets such that X=U‾∪V‾X = \overline{U}\cup \overline{V}, and so U‾\overline{U} is open.
